arXiv:0812.4623v1 [cond-mat.other] 25 Dec 2008

Turing patterns in two dimensional reaction-diffusion system: effect of an electric field

B K Agarwalla Note: bijay.physics@gmail.com Affiliation: Department of Physics, IIT Bombay, Mumbai 400076, India    J K Bhattacharjee Note: jkb@bose.res.in Affiliation: S.N.Bose National Centre for Basic Sciences, JD Block, Sector III, Salt lake city, Kolkata 700098, India    P Titum Affiliation: Department of Physics, IIT Kanpur, 208016, India
Abstract

We consider a two dimensional Turing like system with two diffusing species which interact with each other. Considering the species to be charged, we include the effect of an electric field along a given direction which can lead to a drift induced instability found by A.B.Rovinsky and M.Menzinger[9]. This allows one to study the competition between diffusion and drift as was done numerically by Riaz et al. We show here that an analytic formula can be found on the basis of a linear stability analysis that incorporates all the effects that are known for the system and also allows for some detailed predictions.

Pattern formation in two reacting and diffusing species was first studied by Turing[1, 2]. Turing argued that if the diffusion coefficients of the two species are widely different, then if one of the species is auto catalytic with the other inhibiting its growth, then the steady homogeneous state will be unstable to a patterned steady state. The instability could also set in as a temporal pattern in a spatially homogeneous state under certain conditions. Turing patterns have been a very important aspect of the study of nonlinear systems[3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. Decades later it was found by Rovinsky and Menzinger [9, 10, 11] that pattern formation could occur even if the two diffusion coefficients were nearly equal provided there was an external electric field and the diffusion species were charged giving rise to a gradient coupling. The pattern formed in this case would be travelling waves as opposed to the standing waves of the Turing pattern. Recently there has been extension of the Turing work in some unexpected directions [12, 13]. In a recent study, Riaz et al[14, 15] have shown numerically that a Turing pattern for charged species could be altered by an applied electric field [16].

In this work, we revisit the pattern formation problem with an external electric field to arrive at a single analytic result that has the property of capturing all the possible conditions for the instabilities in the system. We work with a two dimensional set up as in the work of Riaz et al. We take the system to be unbounded in the yy direction and be bounded by rigid plates at x=±Lx=\pm L. The boundary conditions are that the concentration of the species vanishes at the boundary and so does the current normal to the plates which is proportional to the xx-derivative of the concentrations. The electric field is taken to be in the xx direction which leads to a drift in that direction. The existence of the plates in the xx-direction is vital to keep the system bounded. The plates also play the very important role of fixing the wave number in the xx-direction. In the absence of the constraint there will be an overall selection mechanism for the wave numbers (𝐤=𝐤𝟏+𝐤𝟐{\bf k=k_{1}+k_{2}}) but the individual components are not uniquely determined. What we will see below is that k1k_{1} is fixed by the boundary condition and thus once k2k^{2} is known both k1k_{1}and k2k_{2} will be determined. In the work of Riaz et al[14] the fixing of k1k_{1} and k2k_{2} is undertaken numerically. Here the analytic fixing of k1k_{1} allows us to find a general expression for the thresholds of the different instabilities.

The general reaction-diffusion problem for two species A⁡(x,y,t)A(x,y,t) and B⁡(x,y,t)B(x,y,t) can be modelled by the evalutaion equation[14]

∂A∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial A}{\partial t} =\displaystyle= D​∇2A+z2​E​D​∂A∂x+f⁡(A,B)\displaystyle D{\nabla^{2}A}+z_{2}ED\frac{\partial A}{\partial x}+f(A,B) (1)
∂B∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial B}{\partial t} =\displaystyle= ∇2B+z1​E​∂B∂x+g⁡(A,B)\displaystyle{\nabla^{2}B}+z_{1}E\frac{\partial B}{\partial x}+g(A,B) (2)

In the above, DD is the diffusion coefficient for the species AA in units where the diffusion coefficient for the species BB is unity. The external electric field in the xx-direction in denoted by EE and z1z_{1} and z2z_{2} are the charges associated with the inhibitor and the activitor respectively. The operator ∇2\nabla^{2} is two dimensional (pattern on a substrate) and the function f⁡(A,B)f(A,B) and g⁡(A,B)g(A,B) describe the growth and interaction of the species AA and BB. The electric field terms come from an expression for the current together with the relevant Einstein’s relation. In the Gierer-Meinhardt model[17, 18],

f⁡(A,B)\displaystyle f(A,B) =\displaystyle= A2B−A+σ\displaystyle\frac{A^{2}}{B}-A+\sigma (3)
g⁡(A,B)\displaystyle g(A,B) =\displaystyle= μ⁡(A2−B)\displaystyle\mu(A^{2}-B) (4)

The growth rate of AA due to interaction with the substrate is σ\sigma and the natural decay rate for BB is μ\mu. In the Lengyel-Epstein model[19]

f⁡(A,B)\displaystyle f(A,B) =\displaystyle= σ​b​(B−A​B1+B2)\displaystyle\sigma b(B-\frac{AB}{1+B^{2}}) (5)
g⁡(A,B)\displaystyle g(A,B) =\displaystyle= a−B−4​A​B1+B2\displaystyle a-B-\frac{4AB}{1+B^{2}} (6)

where σ\sigma, bb and aa are constants. The homogeneous steady state is A=A0A=A_{0} and B=B0B=B_{0} such that f⁡(A0,B0)=g⁡(A0,B0)=0f(A_{0},B_{0})=g(A_{0},B_{0})=0. The linear stability analysis around A=A0A=A_{0} and B=B0B=B_{0} leads to

d​δ​Ad​t\displaystyle\frac{d\delta A}{dt} =\displaystyle= D​∇2δ​A+z2​E​D​∂(δ​A)∂x+a11​δ​A+a12​δ​B\displaystyle D\nabla^{2}\delta A+z_{2}ED\frac{\partial(\delta A)}{\partial x}+a_{11}\delta A+a_{12}\delta B (7)
d​δ​Bd​t\displaystyle\frac{d\delta B}{dt} =\displaystyle= ∇2δ​B+z1​E​∂(δ​B)∂x+a21​δ​A+a22​δ​B\displaystyle\nabla^{2}\delta B+z_{1}E\frac{\partial(\delta B)}{\partial x}+a_{21}\delta A+a_{22}\delta B (8)

where a11=(∂f∂A)A0,B0a_{11}=\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial A}\right)_{A_{0},B_{0}}, a12=(∂f∂B)A0,B0a_{12}=\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial B}\right)_{A_{0},B_{0}}, a21=(∂g∂A)A0,B0a_{21}=\left(\frac{\partial g}{\partial A}\right)_{A_{0},B_{0}} and a22=(∂g∂B)A0,B0a_{22}=\left(\frac{\partial g}{\partial B}\right)_{A_{0},B_{0}}

We consider a geometry which is confined by plates at x=±Lx=\pm L and is unbounded in the yy-direction. The solution will be periodic in the yy-direction and if we take the wavenumber in this direction to be k2k_{2}, then we can write

(δ​A,δ​B)=(A1​(x),B1​(x))​exp⁡(i​k2​y)​exp⁡(λ​t)(\delta A,\delta B)=(A_{1}(x),B_{1}(x))\exp{(ik_{2}y)}\exp{(\lambda t)} (9)

where λ\lambda is the eigenvalue determining the temporal growth. Then A1​(x)A_{1}(x) and B1​(x)B_{1}(x) satisfy the differential equation

At this point the general procedure should be clear. We need to solve the homogeneous 4th order equation above. This will involve four arbitrary constants which have to be fixed by boundary conditions. Since the system is homogeneous the four conditions will lead to four homogeneous linear algebraic equations and for consistency the determinant has to vanish. The resulting equation fixes λ\lambda in terms of LL, k2k_{2}, EE and other system parameters. The requirement R​e​λ≥0Re{\lambda}\geq 0 for instability allows us to discuss the different situation that can occur. The above procedure in general and in principle cumbersome. We illustrate this in the simpler situation of E=0E=0 and the Turing limit i.e. D<<1D<<1. The lesson that we learn here will be put to good use for the more complicated case.

m1​tan⁡(m1​L)=m2​tan⁡(m2​L)m_{1}\tan(m_{1}L)=m_{2}\tan(m_{2}L) (20)

using α1\alpha_{1}, α2\alpha_{2}, β1\beta_{1}, β2\beta_{2} given in eq.(27) leads after straightforward algebra to the central result

This is the single formula that contains all the possibilites of the pattern formation in the presence of the electric field.

We will now discuss the various possibilities.

First consider the Turing problem E=0E=0. Now, the right hand side of eq.(29) has to be negative for stability which means

Δ−k2​(a11+D​a22)+D​k4>0\Delta-k^{2}(a_{11}+Da_{22})+Dk^{4}>0 (30)

for stability. This is the central criterion for stability for all Δ>0\Delta>0 in the presence of diffusion. If the sign is reversed in eq.(30), we get the Turing instability and for Δ>0\Delta>0, this occurs for a band of wavenumber where the above expression is negative. The minimum of the expression is obtained for k2=a11+D​a222​Dk^{2}=\frac{a_{11}+Da_{22}}{2D} and the value at the minimum is Δ−(a11+D​a22)24​D\Delta-\frac{(a_{11}+Da_{22})^{2}}{4D} and hence the instability criterion is Δ<(a11+D​a22)24​D\Delta<\frac{(a_{11}+Da_{22})^{2}}{4D} , an inequality which is easy to satisfy for D<<1D<<1

We now consider the opposite limit i.e. there is no diffusion and only drift. In this case eq.(29) acquires the form

(z1−D​z2)2​a11​a22​π24​L2​E2>(T​r​A)2​(−Δ)(z_{1}-Dz_{2})^{2}a_{11}a_{22}\frac{\pi^{2}}{4L^{2}}E^{2}>(TrA)^{2}(-\Delta) (31)

π​E2​L<|T​r​A||z1−D​z2|​(−Δa11​a22)12\frac{\pi E}{2L}<\frac{|TrA|}{|z_{1}-Dz_{2}|}\left(\frac{-\Delta}{a_{11}a_{22}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} (32)

>(T​r​A−2​k2)2​[k2​(a11+a22)−Δ−k4]\displaystyle>(TrA-2k^{2})^{2}[k^{2}(a_{11}+a_{22})-\Delta-k^{4}] (34)

With a11​a22<0a_{11}a_{22}<0 and T​r​A<0TrA<0, we can satisfy this inequality in the range 0≤k≤k00\leq k\leq k_{0} where

2​k02=T​r​A+(T​r​A)2−4​a11​a222k_{0}^{2}=TrA+\sqrt{(TrA)^{2}-4a_{11}a_{22}} (35)

and for k<k0k<k_{0}, the critical value of EE which will trigger an instability will be given by

π24​L2​E2>(T​r​A−2​k2)2(z1−z2)2​k2​(a11+a22)−Δ−k4a11​a22−k2​(a11+a22)+k4\frac{\pi^{2}}{4L^{2}}E^{2}>\frac{(TrA-2k^{2})^{2}}{(z_{1}-z_{2})^{2}}\frac{k^{2}(a_{11}+a_{22})-\Delta-k^{4}}{a_{11}a_{22}-k^{2}(a_{11}+a_{22})+k^{4}} (36)

According to the above relation all wavenumbers greater than k0k_{0} are always stable. In writing down the above condition, we see the advantage of the exact expression of eq.(29). The order of magnitude estimation in [9] does not yield the above answer.

For any DD, we note that if diffusion destabilizes a stable reactive system, then k2​(a11+D​a22)−Δ−D​k4>0k^{2}(a_{11}+Da_{22})-\Delta-Dk^{4}>0 and it follows that a11​a22−k2​(a11+D​a22)+D​k4=a11​a22−Δ+[Δ−k2​(a11+D​a22)+D​k4]<0a_{11}a_{22}-k^{2}(a_{11}+Da_{22})+Dk^{4}=a_{11}a_{22}-\Delta+[\Delta-k^{2}(a_{11}+Da_{22})+Dk^{4}]<0 since a11​a22<0a_{11}a_{22}<0. Hence eq.(29) can never be satisfied. No amount of electric field can stabilize the system. Finally, if the diffusive system is stable i.e. k2​(a11+D​a22)−Δ−D​k4<0k^{2}(a_{11}+Da_{22})-\Delta-Dk^{4}<0, then a critical E⁡(Ec)E(E_{c}) will destabilize the state provided a11​a22−k2​(a11+D​a22)+D​k4<0a_{11}a_{22}-k^{2}(a_{11}+Da_{22})+Dk^{4}<0 which will happen if k<k0′k<k_{0}^{{}^{\prime}} given by

k02′=a11+D​a22+(a11+D​a22)2−4​D​a11​a222​Dk_{0}^{{}^{\prime}2}=\frac{a_{11}+Da_{22}+\sqrt{(a_{11}+Da_{22})^{2}-4Da_{11}a_{22}}}{2D} (37)

For small enough DD, k02′≃(a11+D​a22)Dk_{0}^{{}^{\prime}2}\simeq\frac{(a_{11}+Da_{22})}{D} and

π24​L2​Ec2≃[T​r​A−(1+D)​k2]2(z1−D​z2)2​(−Δa11​a22)\frac{\pi^{2}}{4L^{2}}E_{c}^{2}\simeq\frac{[TrA-(1+D)k^{2}]^{2}}{(z_{1}-Dz_{2})^{2}}\left(\frac{-\Delta}{a_{11}a_{22}}\right) (38)

In summary we have studied a reaction-diffusion system in the presence of a constant electric field along a particular direction. We have found a single analytic expression which contains all possible information about the stability and the instability of the system for different ranges of the diffusion coeffecient. The primary result that emerges is that there is an uppar limit on the wave number of the instability and that for each wave number below that there is a critical electric field that can excite that particular wave number.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research.
